column9: A verb plus object, so it splits: 發了怒, 發什麼怒. 發 here means to let out a feeling, as in 發火, 發脾氣, 發愁.

column3: A verb plus object, so you heave a sigh: 叹了一口气, 叹口气. The sigh comes from sadness, helplessness or relief.
column6: Bié tànqì le, míngtiān huì gèng hǎo.
column7: Stop sighing; tomorrow will be better.
column9: A verb plus object, so you heave a sigh: 嘆了一口氣, 嘆口氣. The sigh comes from sadness, helplessness or relief.

column3: To touch someone's feelings or win them over. The person moved is the object or the subject of 被: 打动人心, 被…打动.
column6: Zhè shǒu gē dǎdòng le hěn duō rén.
column7: This song moved many people.
column9: To touch someone's feelings or win them over. The person moved is the object or the subject of 被: 打動人心, 被…打動.

column3: Mostly before a noun: 难忘的一天, or 令人难忘, 终生难忘. 难 before a verb means hard to do it (难懂, 难忘) or unpleasant to (难吃 tastes bad, 难看 ugly).
column6: Nà shì yī gè nánwàng de yèwǎn.
column7: That was an unforgettable evening.
column9: Mostly before a noun: 難忘的一天, or 令人難忘, 終生難忘. 難 before a verb means hard to do it (難懂, 難忘) or unpleasant to (難吃 tastes bad, 難看 ugly).

column3: A heartfelt wish you hope to fulfill: 实现心愿, 了却心愿 (to settle a long-held wish). More personal than 愿望.
column6: Wǒ de xīnyuàn shì huányóu shìjiè.
column7: My wish is to travel around the world.
column9: A heartfelt wish you hope to fulfill: 實現心願, 了卻心願 (to settle a long-held wish). More personal than 願望.

column3: Formal letter closing: it sits on its own line near the end, and the salutation, usually 敬礼, goes on the next line.
column4: 信的最后，他写上了“此致敬礼”。
column5: 信的最後，他寫上了「此致敬禮」。
column6: Xìn de zuìhòu, tā xiě shàng le “cǐzhì jìnglǐ”.
column7: At the end of the letter he wrote the formal closing.
column9: Formal letter closing: it sits on its own line near the end, and the salutation, usually 敬禮, goes on the next line.

column3: Used to address a group, typically at the start of a speech or announcement. It is polite and a little formal, and never used for one person.
column6: Zhūwèi qǐng zuò.
column7: Everyone, please sit down.
column9: Used to address a group, typically at the start of a speech or announcement. It is polite and a little formal, and never used for one person.

column3: A verb plus its object: the person who gets the seat comes first with 给, as in 给老人让座. It is the standard phrase for giving up your seat on a bus or train. 座 is formed from the word for sitting and is literally “that which is sat on”.
column6: Tā gěi lǎorén ràngzuò le.
column7: He gave up his seat to an elderly person.
column9: A verb plus its object: the person who gets the seat comes first with 給, as in 給老人讓座. It is the standard phrase for giving up your seat on a bus or train. 座 is formed from the word for sitting and is literally “that which is sat on”.

column3: The object is usually a group that needs care: 关爱儿童, 关爱老人. It is warm and a little formal, the tone of campaigns, schools and speeches rather than a word between friends.
column6: Wǒmen yào guān'ài lǎorén.
column7: We should care for the elderly.
column9: The object is usually a group that needs care: 關愛兒童, 關愛老人. It is warm and a little formal, the tone of campaigns, schools and speeches rather than a word between friends.

column3: Describes the loyalty of a servant, soldier, official or pet to a master or country: 对主人忠心. The set phrase 忠心耿耿 means loyal to the core.
column6: Zhè zhī gǒu duì zhǔrén hěn zhōngxīn.
column7: This dog is very loyal to its owner.
column9: Describes the loyalty of a servant, soldier, official or pet to a master or country: 對主人忠心. The set phrase 忠心耿耿 means loyal to the core.

column3: Describes what is surprising in a delightful or mysterious way, often before a noun with 的: 奇妙的世界, 奇妙的感觉, 奇妙的缘分. It does not simply mean excellent.
column6: Zhè shì yī cì qímiào de lǚxíng.
column7: This was a wonderful trip.
column9: Describes what is surprising in a delightful or mysterious way, often before a noun with 的: 奇妙的世界, 奇妙的感覺, 奇妙的緣分. It does not simply mean excellent.

column3: Used for sights on a grand scale that fill the eye: a waterfall, a mountain range, a parade, a skyline. Size and force are the point, not prettiness.
column6: Pùbù de jǐngxiàng shífēn zhuàngguān.
column7: The sight of the waterfall is magnificent.
column9: Used for sights on a grand scale that fill the eye: a waterfall, a mountain range, a parade, a skyline. Size and force are the point, not prettiness.

column3: Describes the thing that moves you, not the person who is moved: a story, a scene or a speech is 感人, while you are 感动. Common before a noun: 感人的故事.
column6: Zhè ge gùshi hěn gǎnrén.
column7: This story is very touching.
column9: Describes the thing that moves you, not the person who is moved: a story, a scene or a speech is 感人, while you are 感動. Common before a noun: 感人的故事.

column3: Praise for a person or an achievement: 杰出的科学家, 杰出贡献. It is formal, the language of news, awards and speeches rather than casual talk. In its oldest form 出 showed a foot 止 stepping out of a cave 凵.
column4: 他是一位杰出的科学家。
column5: 他是一位傑出的科學家。
column6: Tā shì yī wèi jiéchū de kēxuéjiā.
column7: He is an outstanding scientist.
column9: Praise for a person or an achievement: 傑出的科學家, 傑出貢獻. It is formal, the language of news, awards and speeches rather than casual talk. In its oldest form 出 showed a foot 止 stepping out of a cave 凵.

column3: Used before a noun for people, brands and companies that many have heard of: 知名企业, 知名作家. It is formal; in everyday talk 有名 is more usual. One explanation: 名 puts a moon 夕 and a mouth 口 together, saying your name to identify yourself in the dark.
column6: Tā shì yī wèi zhīmíng de zuòjiā.
column7: He is a well-known writer.
column9: Used before a noun for people, brands and companies that many have heard of: 知名企業, 知名作家. It is formal; in everyday talk 有名 is more usual. One explanation: 名 puts a moon 夕 and a mouth 口 together, saying your name to identify yourself in the dark.

column3: Mostly a building block: 精彩, 精神, 精确, 精力, 妖精. On its own in speech it means shrewd, quick to look after one's own interests: 他很精.
column6: Tā zuò shēngyi hěn jīng.
column7: He is shrewd in business.
column9: Mostly a building block: 精彩, 精神, 精確, 精力, 妖精. On its own in speech it means shrewd, quick to look after one's own interests: 他很精.

column3: Describes goods and services, such as 优质产品, 优质服务 and 优质大米; it is the usual word on labels and in ads. The opposite is 劣质.
column6: Zhè jiā diàn zhǐ mài yōuzhì shuǐguǒ.
column7: This shop sells only high-quality fruit.
column9: Describes goods and services, such as 優質產品, 優質服務 and 優質大米; it is the usual word on labels and in ads. The opposite is 劣質.

column3: The good name you can protect or damage: 损害名誉, 名誉受损. Before a title it means honorary: 名誉教授, 名誉主席.
column6: Tā hěn àixī zìjǐ de míngyù.
column7: He guards his reputation carefully.
column9: The good name you can protect or damage: 損害名譽, 名譽受損. Before a title it means honorary: 名譽教授, 名譽主席.

column3: Playfully naughty, said of children and young animals, with more affection than anger; 调皮 is the closest everyday word. 皮 is drawn as a hand stripping the fur from an animal pelt.
column6: Zhè ge háizi hěn wánpí.
column7: This child is very naughty.
column9: Playfully naughty, said of children and young animals, with more affection than anger; 調皮 is the closest everyday word. 皮 is drawn as a hand stripping the fur from an animal pelt.

column3: Admiring: it praises will, life or resistance that does not give in, as in 顽强的意志 and 顽强拼搏. Its near twin 顽固 is stubborn as a fault.
column6: Tā wánqiáng de huó le xiàlái.
column7: He held on and survived against the odds.
column9: Admiring: it praises will, life or resistance that does not give in, as in 頑強的意志 and 頑強拼搏. Its near twin 頑固 is stubborn as a fault.

column3: Sounds the same as 很 (very) but means fierce and ruthless; you meet it in 凶狠, 狠心 (hard-hearted) and 狠狠地 (fiercely). It can also mean doing something with all one's force.
column6: Tā duì zìjǐ zhēn hěn.
column7: He is really hard on himself.
column9: Sounds the same as 很 (very) but means fierce and ruthless; you meet it in 兇狠, 狠心 (hard-hearted) and 狠狠地 (fiercely). It can also mean doing something with all one's force.

column3: The sense heard every day is the loanword “cool”: 很酷, 太酷了. The old sense of harsh and cruel lives on in compounds such as 残酷 and 酷刑.
column6: Zhè ge fàxíng hěn kù.
column7: This hairstyle is cool.
column9: The sense heard every day is the loanword “cool”: 很酷, 太酷了. The old sense of harsh and cruel lives on in compounds such as 殘酷 and 酷刑.

column3: Fits things as well as people: 残酷的现实, 残酷的竞争, 残酷的战争. For a person who is cold and unfeeling, 冷酷 is the usual word.
column6: Xiànshí yǒushí hěn cánkù.
column7: Reality can be cruel at times.
column9: Fits things as well as people: 殘酷的現實, 殘酷的競爭, 殘酷的戰爭. For a person who is cold and unfeeling, 冷酷 is the usual word.

column3: Often kind: it describes ordinary people and humble lives with respect, as in 平凡的岗位 or 平凡中见伟大. The critical word for mediocre is 平庸.
column4: 他是个平凡的人，但很善良。
column5: 他是個平凡的人，但很善良。
column6: Tā shì ge píngfán de rén, dàn hěn shànliáng.
column7: He is an ordinary person, but a kind one.
column9: Often kind: it describes ordinary people and humble lives with respect, as in 平凡的崗位 or 平凡中見偉大. The critical word for mediocre is 平庸.

column3: Two senses: steady and down-to-earth in work (他做事很踏实), and at ease in the mind (心里踏实). Pronounced tāshi on the mainland and tàshí in Taiwan.
column6: Tā zuò shì hěn tāshi.
column7: He works in a steady, down-to-earth way.
column9: Two senses: steady and down-to-earth in work (他做事很踏實), and at ease in the mind (心裡踏實). Pronounced tāshi on the mainland and tàshí in Taiwan.

column3: A written, slightly formal verb that always takes another verb after it: 敢于承认, 敢于挑战. Speech uses plain 敢, and 敢于 praises courage. In its oldest form 敢 showed a hand using a capturing tool to hunt a wild boar.
column6: Wǒmen yào gǎnyú miànduì kùnnan.
column7: We must dare to face difficulties.
column9: A written, slightly formal verb that always takes another verb after it: 敢於承認, 敢於挑戰. Speech uses plain 敢, and 敢於 praises courage. In its oldest form 敢 showed a hand using a capturing tool to hunt a wild boar.

column3: Describes a dominant party, as in 强势品牌 and 强势货币. Of a person it can mean pushy or domineering, so it is not always praise.
column6: Tā zài tánpàn zhōng hěn qiángshì.
column7: He was very forceful in the negotiation.
column9: Describes a dominant party, as in 強勢品牌 and 強勢貨幣. Of a person it can mean pushy or domineering, so it is not always praise.

column3: Physical strength of a body: people, animals, muscles. Strength of a country or a company is 强大, not 强壮. Its older form 彊 was built with a bow 弓, because “Bow is powerful.”
column6: Tā zhǎng de yòu gāo yòu qiángzhuàng.
column7: He is tall and strong.
column9: Physical strength of a body: people, animals, muscles. Strength of a country or a company is 強大, not 強壯. Its older form 彊 was built with a bow 弓, because “Bow is powerful.”

column3: The word for turning a corner when giving directions: 往左拐, 在路口拐弯. It also means to kidnap or swindle, as in 拐骗, and gives 拐杖 (a walking stick).
column6: Dào qiánmiàn lùkǒu wǎng zuǒ guǎi.
column7: Turn left at the intersection ahead.
column9: The word for turning a corner when giving directions: 往左拐, 在路口拐彎. It also means to kidnap or swindle, as in 拐騙, and gives 拐杖 (a walking stick).

column3: To tilt the head back: 仰头看, 仰望, 仰卧 (lie on one's back). Looking up becomes respect in 敬仰 and 仰慕, and belief in 信仰.
column6: Tā yǎng tóu kàn zhe tiānkōng.
column7: He looked up at the sky.
column9: To tilt the head back: 仰頭看, 仰望, 仰臥 (lie on one's back). Looking up becomes respect in 敬仰 and 仰慕, and belief in 信仰.

column3: Both literal (低头看手机) and figurative: 向困难低头 means to give in to difficulties, and 不低头 means refusing to yield.
column6: Tā dītóu kàn shǒujī.
column7: He looks down at his phone.
column9: Both literal (低頭看手機) and figurative: 向困難低頭 means to give in to difficulties, and 不低頭 means refusing to yield.

column3: Turning or twisting that strains: 扭头 turns the head away, 扭伤 is a sprain, and 扭转 turns a situation around.
column6: Wǒ de jiǎo niǔ le.
column7: I twisted my ankle.
column9: Turning or twisting that strains: 扭頭 turns the head away, 扭傷 is a sprain, and 扭轉 turns a situation around.

column3: Fits things with length: roads, rivers, wires, a spine (弯曲的小路, 脊柱弯曲). A person bending at the waist is 弯腰 instead. 曲 is drawn as a bent object.
column6: Zhè tiáo lù wānqū de hěn lìhai.
column7: This road winds a lot.
column9: Fits things with length: roads, rivers, wires, a spine (彎曲的小路, 脊柱彎曲). A person bending at the waist is 彎腰 instead. 曲 is drawn as a bent object.

column3: To hold up from below with the palm: 托着下巴 is resting your chin on your hand. It also means to ask a favor, as in 托你一件事 and 拜托.
column6: Tā yòng shǒu tuō zhe xiàba.
column7: He rests his chin on his hand.
column9: To hold up from below with the palm: 托著下巴 is resting your chin on your hand. It also means to ask a favor, as in 托你一件事 and 拜託.

column3: The 走 shows the thing leaving the speaker's place: 拿走 is take it away, while 拿来 is bring it here. 走 began as a picture of a running man.
column4: 请不要拿走别人的东西。
column5: 請不要拿走別人的東西。
column6: Qǐng bù yào názǒu biérén de dōngxi.
column7: Please do not take other people's things.
column9: The 走 shows the thing leaving the speaker's place: 拿走 is take it away, while 拿來 is bring it here. 走 began as a picture of a running man.

column3: With this reading, 背着 usually means doing something behind someone's back: 背着父母, 背着我. Hands held behind the back is 背着手. Carrying a load on the back is the other reading, bēizhe.
column4: 他背着父母偷偷出去了。
column5: 他背著父母偷偷出去了。
column6: Tā bèizhe fùmǔ tōutōu chūqù le.
column7: He slipped out behind his parents' backs.
column9: With this reading, 背著 usually means doing something behind someone's back: 背著父母, 背著我. Hands held behind the back is 背著手. Carrying a load on the back is the other reading, bēizhe.

column3: 着 makes the pointing last while something else happens: 指着地图说, 指着我问. The thing pointed at follows directly; 指着鼻子骂 is rude, scolding someone to their face.
column4: 他指着地图问我们在哪儿。
column5: 他指著地圖問我們在哪兒。
column6: Tā zhǐzhe dìtú wèn wǒmen zài nǎr.
column7: He pointed at the map and asked where we were.
column9: 著 makes the pointing last while something else happens: 指著地圖說, 指著我問. The thing pointed at follows directly; 指著鼻子罵 is rude, scolding someone to their face.

column3: To be right up against something: 挨着窗户坐, 紧挨着. The same 挨 read ái means to suffer, as in 挨骂 and 挨打, so the reading matters.
column6: Tā āizhe wǒ zuò xià le.
column7: He sat down next to me.
column9: To be right up against something: 挨著窗戶坐, 緊挨著. The same 挨 read ái means to suffer, as in 挨罵 and 挨打, so the reading matters.

column3: Read zhā for pricking and settling in: 扎针 (get a shot or acupuncture), 扎根 (take root), 扎营. Other readings are zā, to tie (扎辫子), and zhá in 挣扎.
column6: Shǒuzhǐ bèi zhēn zhā le yī xià.
column7: A needle pricked my finger.
column9: Read zhā for pricking and settling in: 扎針 (get a shot or acupuncture), 扎根 (take root), 紮營. Other readings are zā, to tie (扎辮子), and zhá in 掙扎.

column3: Adds something extra to what is already there: 添饭 (a refill of rice), 添水, 添麻烦 (to trouble someone). In math and for plain addition the word is 加.
column6: Qǐng zài gěi wǒ tiān diǎn shuǐ.
column7: Please top up my water.
column9: Adds something extra to what is already there: 添飯 (a refill of rice), 添水, 添麻煩 (to trouble someone). In math and for plain addition the word is 加.

column3: Read chòng, it means facing or aimed at someone: 冲着他笑, 冲我来. It also means strong or pungent, as in 味儿很冲. The common reading chōng is to rush, rinse or flush.
column6: Tā chòng wǒ xiào le xiào.
column7: She smiled at me.
column9: Read chòng, it means facing or aimed at someone: 衝著他笑, 衝我來. It also means strong or pungent, as in 味兒很衝. The common reading chōng is to rush, rinse or flush.

column3: Rarely used alone. It is mostly a suffix naming a shape, as in 圆形, 三角形, 长方形, or sits in words such as 形状, 形成, 情形.
column6: Zhè zhāng zhuōzi shì yuán xíng de.
column7: This table is round.
column9: Rarely used alone. It is mostly a suffix naming a shape, as in 圓形, 三角形, 長方形, or sits in words such as 形狀, 形成, 情形.

column3: Either an accident or a trick: things warp from heat, water or pressure (木门变形), and 变形金刚 is the Transformers toys and films.
column6: Mùmén bèi shuǐ pào de biànxíng le.
column7: The wooden door warped from soaking in water.
column9: Either an accident or a trick: things warp from heat, water or pressure (木門變形), and 變形金剛 is the Transformers toys and films.

column3: Spacious and open: roads, squares, rivers, the sea, and figuratively a broad mind (胸怀宽阔). It gives a feeling of open space, not a measurement.
column6: Zhè tiáo lù yòu zhí yòu kuānkuò.
column7: This road is straight and wide.
column9: Spacious and open: roads, squares, rivers, the sea, and figuratively a broad mind (胸懷寬闊). It gives a feeling of open space, not a measurement.

column3: Rarely a word on its own: wide inside 宽阔, 广阔 and 辽阔. In speech it also means newly rich and showy, as in 阔气 and 阔起来.
column4: 他发财以后就阔起来了。
column5: 他發財以後就闊起來了。
column6: Tā fācái yǐhòu jiù kuò qǐlái le.
column7: After he got rich, he began living it up.
column9: Rarely a word on its own: wide inside 寬闊, 廣闊 and 遼闊. In speech it also means newly rich and showy, as in 闊氣 and 闊起來.

column3: Grand in scale and ambition: 宏大的计划, 宏大的规模, 宏大的场面. It is written and slightly formal, and it stresses grandeur rather than plain size: a building can be 宏大, but a big apple is just 大.
column4: 他们有一个宏大的计划。
column5: 他們有一個宏大的計劃。
column6: Tāmen yǒu yī ge hóngdà de jìhuà.
column7: They have a grand plan.
column9: Grand in scale and ambition: 宏大的計劃, 宏大的規模, 宏大的場面. It is written and slightly formal, and it stresses grandeur rather than plain size: a building can be 宏大, but a big apple is just 大.

column3: Appears in labels and news: 特大暴雨 (a top-grade rainstorm), 特大号 (extra large), 特大城市 (a megacity). It is stronger than plain 大.
column6: Jīntiān yǒu tèdà bàoyǔ.
column7: There is a torrential rainstorm today.
column9: Appears in labels and news: 特大暴雨 (a top-grade rainstorm), 特大號 (extra large), 特大城市 (a megacity). It is stronger than plain 大.

column3: Besides measured length, it means a mishap in 万一有个长短 (if anything should happen), and 说长道短 is gossiping about people's good and bad points. 长 began as a picture of an old man with long hair.
column4: 这两根绳子长短不一样。
column5: 這兩根繩子長短不一樣。
column6: Zhè liǎng gēn shéngzi chángduǎn bù yīyàng.
column7: These two ropes are not the same length.
column9: Besides measured length, it means a mishap in 萬一有個長短 (if anything should happen), and 說長道短 is gossiping about people's good and bad points. 長 began as a picture of an old man with long hair.

column3: 通 adds “all the way through”, so the whole face, ears or iron is red: 脸通红, 冻得通红. It usually follows 得 after the cause: 羞得通红.
column6: Tā de liǎn xiū de tōnghóng.
column7: His face turned bright red from embarrassment.
column9: 通 adds “all the way through”, so the whole face, ears or iron is red: 臉通紅, 凍得通紅. It usually follows 得 after the cause: 羞得通紅.

column3: Polite and formal: 行动不便 (limited mobility), 多有不便 (apologizing for the trouble), 不便透露 (not appropriate to disclose). In casual talk 不方便 is used.
column6: Lǎorén xíngdòng bùbiàn.
column7: The old man has trouble getting around.
column9: Polite and formal: 行動不便 (limited mobility), 多有不便 (apologizing for the trouble), 不便透露 (not appropriate to disclose). In casual talk 不方便 is used.

column3: Roads, pipes and noses can be 不通 (blocked). Writing or an argument that is 不通 makes no sense, and 行不通 says a plan will not work. 不 began as a picture of the calyx of a flower; its meaning “no” came through 否, which was built on it.
column6: Zhè tiáo lù bùtōng.
column7: This road is blocked.
column9: Roads, pipes and noses can be 不通 (blocked). Writing or an argument that is 不通 makes no sense, and 行不通 says a plan will not work. 不 began as a picture of the calyx of a flower; its meaning “no” came through 否, which was built on it.

column3: It is often used with 得 and a verb, as in 不值得去 (not worth going), and in set phrases: 不值钱 (worthless) and 不值一提 (not worth mentioning).
column6: Zhè diǎn xiǎo shì bùzhí yī tí.
column7: This small matter is not worth mentioning.
column9: It is often used with 得 and a verb, as in 不值得去 (not worth going), and in set phrases: 不值錢 (worthless) and 不值一提 (not worth mentioning).

column3: Softens a negative before a verb or adjective: 不怎么好 (not that good), 不怎么喜欢 (don't like it much). It does not ask how.
column6: Wǒ bùzěnme xǐhuan chī là.
column7: I don't really like spicy food.
column9: Softens a negative before a verb or adjective: 不怎麼好 (not that good), 不怎麼喜歡 (don't like it much). It does not ask how.

column3: It stands at the end as a verdict: 这家餐厅不怎么样 (nothing special), a mild way to say poor. As an answer to “how was it?” it means so-so.
column6: Zhè bù diànyǐng bùzěnmeyàng.
column7: This movie is nothing special.
column9: It stands at the end as a verdict: 這家餐廳不怎麼樣 (nothing special), a mild way to say poor. As an answer to “how was it?” it means so-so.

column3: Followed by a verb: a feeling or action bursts out that you cannot stop, as in 不禁笑了, 不禁想起. It is more common in writing and storytelling than in plain speech.
column4: 听到这个消息，他不禁笑了。
column5: 聽到這個消息，他不禁笑了。
column6: Tīng dào zhè ge xiāoxi, tā bùjīn xiào le.
column7: Hearing the news, he could not help smiling.
column9: Followed by a verb: a feeling or action bursts out that you cannot stop, as in 不禁笑了, 不禁想起. It is more common in writing and storytelling than in plain speech.
